No matching assumption in WE-018; judged from the text: carryout bags are a small part of what retailers sell, so the stores keep selling their goods and their staff are not tied to bags.

No matching assumption in WE-018; judged from the text: shoppers near the edge already shop across the line, so buying bags there takes no extra trip.

No row with a probability in WE-018; judged from the text. Section 2 classifies K2 as binding: without the minimum charge, stores would give paper bags away free to compete, as they gave thin bags (about 2 cents each) away before.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-018 (illustrative figures), A-1: most retailers comply, chains in particular. C-2 and C-6 rest on this assumption alone.

No separate row in WE-018; judged from the text. Shoppers who take a paper bag pay at least 10 cents where they paid nothing, and no other term can offset it (C-2 and C-6 both rest on A-1 alone). The reusable-bag route is a substitute (A-2), not an offset of the price of the paper bag. Same figure as A-1, on which C-2 depends.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-018 (illustrative figures), A-5: some small stores keep handing out thin bags, or waive the fee, without being caught. The fee waiver is trade below the floor.

No matching assumption in WE-018; judged from the text. The bound buyers of the paper bag are shoppers, each paying a few cents a trip; A-8 names bag makers and retailers as the groups that can organize, not shoppers (same reading as k1.buyers_organize).

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-018 (illustrative figures), A-8: bag makers and retailers can organize at a cost below their stake. Section 5 (C-11) names retailers lobbying over the fee.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-018 (illustrative figures), A-6: some shoppers near Route 9 are close to indifferent between stores on either side of the line. Section 5 (C-9) explains the crossing by the fee.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-018 (illustrative figures), A-2: shoppers accept reusable and paper bags as substitutes. Reusable bags may be sold at any price, so they are the substitute for the paper bag at the floor.
